text: Course one introduced Service Request Management as an ITIL practice — the idea that routine, pre-approved requests shouldn't flow through the same unstructured intake as an incident. The Service Catalog is where that concept becomes a real, administered object. Every catalog item a requester can browse and order is a row on the sc_cat_item table, and building the catalog out means populating that table accurately.

A catalog item record carries fields a non-technical requester actually needs to make a decision: Short description, which shows on the tile; Price, which defaults to zero unless the organization charges IT costs back to departments; and Delivery time, a plain-language expectation set by the admin based on the real fulfillment SLA, shown before the requester ever clicks Order Now.

Above the item sits sc_catalog, the storefront itself. Most organizations run exactly one catalog, simply named Service Catalog, and every orderable item lives inside it. But the platform supports multiple catalogs for genuinely different audiences — an internal employee catalog and a separate customer-facing catalog, say — each with its own branding, its own visible categories, and its own access controls.

Categories, stored on sc_category, are what a requester actually clicks through before finding an item. Categories are self-referencing: a Parent field on one category record can point to another category record, which is how subcategories like Hardware and then Laptops and Desktops get built without a separate table for every level of depth. An Order field controls where a category sits relative to its siblings.

Put together, a requester's real path is: open a catalog, click through one or more categories from parent to child, land on a specific catalog item, read its short description, price, and delivery time, and then click Order Now. Getting the category tree right matters — a flat list of fifty items forces guesswork, and a tree that's too deep adds needless clicks.

None of what follows in this chapter — the variables a requester fills in, the policies that react to their answers, or the records those answers eventually create — happens without a correctly configured item sitting inside a sensibly organized category first. Next up: variables and variable sets, the fields that actually make a request form collect real information.
